readerTitle: Same offer, two years apart: why timing decided the outcome
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주택 수리 업체, 기업 대상 회계 서비스) + 실제 기업 (Webvan) + 실제 관찰 (Bill Gross TED 강연)
insight: 아이디어가 좋은지보다 '지금 무엇이 바뀌었기에 고객이 준비됐는가'를 먼저 묻는다. 타이밍은 운이 아니라 읽을 수 있는 바깥 조건이다.
misconception: 좋은 아이디어와 실행력만 있으면 언제 시작해도 성공한다. 타이밍은 통제할 수 없는 운일 뿐이다.

sources.text: Webvan 파산 보도 (2001년 7월), 예: The New York Times, CNET 등 당시 기사
Bill Gross, "The single biggest reason why startups succeed", TED, 2015
주택 수리 업체, 회계 서비스 업체는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Webvan: 1999년 서비스 시작, 2001년 파산. 대규모 투자를 받아 자동화 물류창고를 지었다는 점은 널리 알려진 내용이나, 투자 금액 등 구체 수치는 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다. 연도를 게시 전 다시 확인하세요.
Bill Gross: TED 강연에서 약 200개 기업을 살펴보니 타이밍이 팀, 아이디어, 자금보다 성패 차이를 더 많이 설명했다고 말함(강연에서 42%라는 수치 언급). 엄밀한 학술 연구가 아닌 투자자의 비공식 분석이라는 점을 카드에 밝혔습니다. 기업 수를 다시 확인하세요.
8번 카드의 전자 세금계산서 의무화 규정은 특정 국가 법률이 아닌 가상의 설정입니다. 법률·세무 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 일반적으로만 표현했습니다.

cards.title: Same offer, two years apart: why timing decided the outcome
body: A home repair company starts offering free video-call estimates. A customer points a phone at the leaking pipe, and a technician quotes the job on the spot.
In the first year, almost nobody books one. A few years later, the same offer fills the calendar. Same company, same price, same service.

image.label: A homeowner showing a leaking pipe to a technician on a phone video call
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 화면을 반으로 나눠 왼쪽은 '그때': 텅 빈 예약 달력과 먼지 쌓인 전화기. 오른쪽은 '지금': 같은 달력이 꽉 차 있고, 주인이 휴대폰으로 싱크대 아래 새는 파이프를 비추며 기술자와 영상 통화 중. 실제 앱이나 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What most likely changed?
body: The company didn't redesign the service or cut the price. Its ads were roughly the same.
Why did the same offer go from ignored to popular?

options.text: The company finally collected enough online reviews
options.feedback: Reviews help, but they build slowly and can't explain a sudden jump. Something bigger was pushing customers.

options.text: Customers got used to video calls in the rest of their lives
options.feedback: Yes. The service stayed the same, but customers changed. Once video calls felt normal at work and with family, one with a plumber felt normal too.

options.text: Competitors raised their prices for in-person visits
options.feedback: Possible, but nothing in the story points to it. Reaching for a price story can hide the real cause: customers weren't ready before.

cards.title: The world moved, not the business.
body: In the early years, video calls felt odd for many people. Some didn't know how to start one. Others felt they should pay for a real visit.
Then video calls became a daily habit almost everywhere. Phone cameras got better, and connections got faster.
The company didn't win by getting smarter. It won because the conditions around its idea finally arrived. Before that, its good idea had nowhere to land.

cards.title: Market timing
body: **Market timing** is whether customers are ready and able to buy your offer at the moment you launch it.

Readiness depends on things outside your business: habits, technology, costs, rules. Launch too early and you pay to change customer behavior on your own. Launch too late and others already own the space.
A useful test is one question: **why now?** What changed recently that makes this work today, and not five years ago?

image.label: A surfer catching a wave at the right moment, with one too early and one too late
image.brief: 서퍼 세 명 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 서퍼는 파도가 오기 전에 일어나 물에 빠짐("Too early"), 가운데 서퍼는 파도 꼭대기를 탐("Right time"), 오른쪽 서퍼는 파도가 지나간 뒤 서 있음("Too late"). 파도에는 "Habits · Technology · Costs · Rules" 라벨.

cards.title: Right idea, wrong decade.
body: Webvan launched online grocery delivery in the US in 1999. It built large automated warehouses, then went bankrupt in 2001.
Grocery delivery later became common, once smartphones, online payment and shopping habits had caught up. The idea wasn't wrong. It was early.

In a 2015 TED talk, investor Bill Gross said that when he reviewed about 200 companies, timing explained more of the difference between success and failure than team, idea or funding. It was his own informal analysis, not a formal study, but it matches what many founders report.

cards.title: Five signs a market is getting ready.
body: Timing isn't pure luck. You can look for changes outside your business:
list: **Habits:** customers already do something similar elsewhere
**Technology:** a tool they need is now cheap or common
**Rules:** a new requirement or permission creates demand
**Infrastructure:** the roads, networks or suppliers now exist
cards.callout: If you can't name one, you may be early.
cards.softwareNote: Many software products only became possible when something underneath them changed, like phones in every pocket or cheap cloud computing. A strong "why now" answer usually names that shift.

cards.title: Timing is a reading, not a prediction.
body: Nobody can pick the perfect month. Hype can look like readiness, and real shifts can take longer than expected.
Timing is also an easy excuse. When an offer fails, "the market wasn't ready" may hide a weak product or the wrong customer.
So test small. Spend little while signals are weak, and spend more once customers start asking without being pushed.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: You serve small business clients. A new rule will require electronic invoices in 18 months. Few clients are asking about it yet.
How do you time a setup-and-training service?

options.text: Hire a full team now and market it heavily
options.feedback: You'd be first, but you'd pay salaries for months while clients still feel no urgency. Demand will likely peak near the deadline.

options.text: Wait until the rule takes effect, then launch
options.feedback: You save money, but the rush comes before the deadline. By then, clients may have booked someone who was ready.

options.text: Build a small offer now and grow it as clients start asking
options.feedback: The rule gives you a clear "why now" and a date. A small start keeps costs low while you watch demand rise toward the deadline.

cards.title: A good idea needs a ready market.
body: Before launching, ask what changed outside your business that makes customers ready now. If nothing has, start small and watch.
**Try it today:** write one sentence that begins "This works now, and not five years ago, because…". If you can't finish it, look again.
